title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Advantages of DSPy.RLM in structured task execution
summary:
Fabulous - Your ReAct agent's tools become normal functions that your RLM can use inside the REPL.
Quoting @isaacbmiller1
DSPy.RLM has been getting more attention with the amazing benchmark results on LongCot by @rawworks.
The big structural advantage that dspy.RLM has over other RLM implementations is Signatures.
Signatures let the RLM be directed in the task that you need it to solve:
1. Inputs are separate, typed variables.
Instead of one giant string, you show the model a preview of the variables, and the Python types that they represent. It doesn’t need to do parsing or exploring to understand the structure of an input, only the content.
2. The model is required to conform to structured outputs
You require the RLM to finish a trajectory by using a typed submit function Instead of being able to submit any string.
This means that when you want the model to do a specific task, it can't just submit anything. It needs to submit values that conform to your type definition.
3. The instructions are directly in the context.
For solving a real task, you do don’t want the entirety of the prompt to be inside of a variable. You do want the long inputs to be in a variable, but shorter instructions don’t give you much benefit from being discovered rather than shown in the prompt.
Bonus: Your ReAct agent's tools become normal functions that your RLM can use inside the REPL.
I talked about these advantages at the last DSPy meetup. See my talk below!

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Using RLM with a Python REPL for LLM exploration
summary:
RLM is the most import foundation of my Pi Harness (other than Pi of course). It's seeded with late interaction retrieval results (thanks to @lightonai for pylate).
The Agent initiates it with query then..
𝐒𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐩
A python REPL is created and seeded with:
1. Late interaction search to pre-filter. Instead of doing top 3/5/10, it's top hundreds of documents. This is set into a `context` variable.
2. Python functions are loaded in to do more searches if `context` variable isn't enough. And to make llm calls with cheaper models in parallel batches.
𝐈𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐩
From there, an LLM iterates in the REPL based on the query. It's just like exploring in a jupyter notebook. The LLM writes prose (like a markdown cell) and code to be run in the REPL each turn.
This allows the LLM to sort, filter, and synthesize information. It can fan out and ask smaller models to summarize, combine, contrast, or do anything else to documents to help it understand the data.
After several turns the LLM reponds with the final answer. Either because it found the answer, or hit the budget limit.
Context as a Python variable, LLM as the programmer, REPL as the runtime.
𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐃𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤
1. Richer Shell. Agents (and subagents) work by intermixing code and prose/thinking. But they use static scripts or bash that run and exit and start over each tool call. That's not ideal for exploration and synthesis of data. For that, state is useful to continue building and exploring the data as you learn more. There's a reason jupyter notebooks have been popular with data scientists.
2. Keeps main agent context clean. The better context you have the better the agent will perform (duh!). This means three thing: better human input, less missing search results, and less incorrect search results. Letting the agent iterate allows it to synthesize just what is needed and nothing else. All bad paths or peeks at something that turns out to be irrelevant stays out of main agent context.
3. Stack the good ideas! People often compare late interaction search vs RLM. Or static vs dynamic languages. Or agentic search vs semantic search. But...You can just use them all together for what they're each good at. Use them all for the area they're really great for.
Read the full post which has more detail about how and why.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2048018775904235520/img/TztFazvoexKCnLl1.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2048018775904235520/vid/avc1/480x270/CtgN71ASORS6THyv.mp4?tag=21
clean_summary:
RLM is the most important foundation of my Pi Harness, alongside Pi itself. It's seeded with late interaction retrieval results, thanks to @lightonai for pylate. The Agent initiates it with a query, creating a Python REPL seeded with late interaction search results to pre-filter hundreds of documents into a context variable.

An LLM iterates in the REPL based on the query, similar to exploring in a Jupyter notebook. It writes prose and code to be executed in the REPL, allowing it to sort, filter, and synthesize information. This iterative process helps the LLM respond with a final answer after several turns, either by finding the answer or hitting the budget limit.

This approach works because it creates a richer shell for exploration and synthesis, keeps the main agent context clean, and allows for stacking good ideas from various methodologies. The full post provides more detail about how and why this system functions effectively.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Boosting RLM performance on LongCoT-mini without training
summary:
New mini experiment + blogpost + trajectories!
tldr; we boost performance of RLM(GPT-5.2) to double the best performing number (38.7% --> 65.6%) on LongCoT-mini without any training! An example of the mismanaged geniuses hypothesis (MGH) we (@zli11010, @lateinteraction) proposed earlier this month.
The LongCoT benchmark showed that frontier LMs and RLMs struggled to solve difficult compositional reasoning tasks. The paper generally attributes this to the RLMs inability to perform task decomposition, but we argue this is more our fault in how we prompt them; this capability is fully available to GPT-5.2 with an RLM harness!
Building on @raw_works's insightful blogpost and @sumeetrm / @CharlieLondon02 et al.'s incredibly useful benchmark, where they originally found RLMs to be incapable of solving the MATH and CS splits altogether. We did not train anything since the release of the initial benchmark.
To be fully transparent, these results are not meant to be added to their leaderboard either; benchmarks measure isolated capabilities, and we focus on showing (through different, rather specific prompting) that the capabilities required to solve these tasks are available to the models without additional training! It also has implications about how we would go about training these systems. Full blog below, it's a nice read :)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HG1QTIyaUAA9Poj.jpg

New mini experiment and blog post on boosting the performance of RLM (GPT-5.2) to double the best performing number on LongCoT-mini, from 38.7% to 65.6%, without any training. This illustrates the mismanaged geniuses hypothesis (MGH) proposed earlier this month.

The LongCoT benchmark revealed that frontier LMs and RLMs struggled with difficult compositional reasoning tasks, attributed to RLMs' inability to perform task decomposition. However, the authors argue that this issue stems from how they prompt the models, as GPT-5.2 can handle these tasks effectively with the right RLM harness. The results are not meant for leaderboard inclusion, as they focus on demonstrating that the necessary capabilities are present in the models without additional training.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
We’re introducing HALO 😇
Hierarchal Agent Loop Optimizer
HALO is an RLM-based agent optimization technique capable of recursively self-improving agents by analyzing their execution traces and suggesting changes.
This work is inspired by the Mismanaged Genius Hypothesis proposed by @a1zhang and @lateinteraction earlier this month.
tldr; we improved performance on AppWorld (Sonnet 4.6) from 73.7 --> 89.5 (+15.8) by giving HALO-RLM access to harness trace data and asking it to identify issues.
The feedback from HALO surfaced failures in the harness such as hallucinated tool calls, redundant arguments in tools, refusal loops, and semantic correctness issues. Each issue mapped cleanly to a direct prompt update.
We then fed these finding into Cursor (Opus 4.6), and asked the coding agent to update the underlying harness.
We repeated this trace -> HALO-RLM analysis -> code update loop until the score plateaued.
Today we’re open-sourcing the core HALO-RLM framework, evals, and data for further review.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHG2HCHa4AAvikB.jpg

HALO is an RLM-based agent optimization technique capable of recursively self-improving agents by analyzing their execution traces and suggesting changes.
This work is inspired by the Mismanaged Genius Hypothesis proposed by @a1zhang and @lateinteraction earlier this month.
tldr; we improved performance on AppWorld (Sonnet 4.6) from 73.7 --> 89.5 (+15.8) by giving HALO-RLM access to harness trace data and asking it to identify issues.
The feedback from HALO surfaced failures in the harness such as hallucinated tool calls, redundant arguments in tools, refusal loops, and semantic correctness issues. Each issue mapped cleanly to a direct prompt update.
We then fed these finding into Cursor (Opus 4.6), and asked the coding agent to update the underlying harness.
We repeated this trace -> HALO-RLM analysis -> code update loop until the score plateaued.
Today we’re open-sourcing the core HALO-RLM framework, evals, and data for further review.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Diane releases OBLIQ-Bench, a challenging new IR benchmark with oblique queries
summary:
I’ve never been this excited about search.
6-7 years ago, IR got an influx of the paradigms we still use, all enabled by the big headroom MS MARCO and then BEIR created. Then progress slowed.
Today, Diane releases perhaps the most ambitious IR benchmark to date: OBLIQ-Bench.
Queries in it are meant to be increasingly opaque to current first-stage retrieval paradigms. Oblique queries put the bottleneck very early in the search process, as the relevance of a document to the query is quite latent.
I can't wait for core IR research on fundamentally more powerful paradigms for first-stage search to be reignited again. Stay tuned for more stories about this, and read Diane's thread and her paper below!!
Quoting @dianetc_
We set out to build a better retriever, so we looked for the hardest IR benchmarks.
For each, we asked how much headroom remained by running oracle reranking with a frontier LLM. Most had little room left!
So we built OBLIQ-Bench to study much harder search queries than before.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHpb42wWMAcq-uC.png
clean_summary: Omar Khattab expresses excitement about search and IR progress. He highlights Diane's release of OBLIQ-Bench, an ambitious new benchmark featuring oblique queries designed to be opaque to current first-stage retrieval methods. These queries challenge the relevance signals early in the search process, potentially reigniting core IR research on more powerful paradigms. Diane's team built OBLIQ-Bench to study search queries that leave little room for improvement even with oracle reranking using large language models, marking a step toward more difficult and realistic search scenarios.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Limitations of current retrieval algorithms on real-world hard queries and the OBLIQ-Bench suite
summary:
A little story: Exactly six years and a half and 3 days ago, I had the thrill of stumbling upon the ideas in ColBERT, a then very unusual paradigm for search.
And I've longed for a similar moment ever since, but it was hard to find a hill worth climbing in the same way.
That taught me that the credit for progress in IR in 2019-2020 largely goes to MS MARCO and in 2021 to BEIR, both of which are good benchmarks gave us a solid and unsaturated hill to experiment with fundamentally new paradigms for core retrieval.
But these hills lasted really ~1 year each, and the community is still without a good central hill for the central problem of first-stage search.
Sadly, everyone who’s tried the current generation of retrieval algorithms on real-life hard queries knows they pretty much suck, but they all seem to ace the benchmarks. What's the deal?
A lot of the field started focusing on things I love too, like multi-hop deep research agents. It's a hugely important problem (see Baleen from 2020), but it almost suggests that we think that the core retrieval challenge (i.e., each actual hop!) is now solved. Is it?
These underlying limited retrievers are the search tools you hand to your agents. Your agents can't access information that your retrievers can't find!
Check out @dianetc_'s new OBLIQ-Bench, a suite of five hard, "oblique", and more ambitious search problems, and a reliable way to build many more of them and make them arbitrarily harder.
Diane's key insight here is that as reasoning models become increasingly more powerful by leveraging highly expressive architectures and scaling inference-time compute up for processing each of their prompts, we can begin to define very hard IR problems.
Specifically, problems where reasoning LLMs have no trouble recognizing even very subtle cases of relevant documents when they are shown, but current scalable retrieval systems cannot surface them from the corpus in the first place!
We hope that this can allow the community to go back to one of the few rather "AGI-proof" problems out there: even if you have Einstein in a GPT-6 box, being able to cheaply search billions of documents in milliseconds calls for a very different design space than a big LLM.
Quoting @dianetc_
We set out to build a better retriever, so we looked for the hardest IR benchmarks.
For each, we asked how much headroom remained by running oracle reranking with a frontier LLM. Most had little room left!
So we built OBLIQ-Bench to study much harder search queries than before.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHpb42wWMAcq-uC.png
clean_summary: Omar Khattab reflects on the progress and challenges in information retrieval over the past six years, noting that recent benchmarks like MS MARCO and BEIR provided clear hills for experimentation, but these have been short-lived. Despite advances, current retrieval systems perform poorly on difficult real-life queries, even though they excel on benchmarks. Diane's OBLIQ-Bench suite introduces more challenging search problems that reveal the limited ability of scalable retrieval systems to surface relevant documents, especially as reasoning models grow more powerful. This work aims to push retrieval research toward solving more complex, 'AGI-proof' search problems that require fundamentally different system designs to handle billions of documents efficiently.

Experiments show that existing models struggle with these challenges, suggesting directions for future development to improve retrieval robustness and accuracy.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Fast-Slow Training: Interleaving context and weight optimization for efficient LLM learning
summary:
Learning from rich textual feedback (errors, traces, partial reasoning) beats scalar reward alone for LLM optimization. GEPA demonstrated this for context-space optimization (prompts and agent harnesses), delivering frontier results at a fraction of the cost of RL.
But context-only optimization is bounded by the base model's capability ceiling; weight updates can reach further.
Very excited about this new line of work on Fast-Slow Training (FST), which interleaves context and model weight optimization!
The idea is a clean division of labor between two interleaved loops:
🔹 Fast loop (context): GEPA reads rich rollout feedback updating the context layer. The context becomes a fast-updating scratchpad of what the model needs to know about this task, right now.
🔹 Slow loop (model parameters): RL updates the model's parameters conditioned on the evolving context. Because the prompt already carries task-specific nuances, the model parameters are freed from absorbing them and focus on what actually generalizes across tasks and pushes the frontier.
⦁ 3× more sample-efficient than RL on math, code, and physics reasoning
⦁ ~70% lower KL divergence from base at matched accuracy
⦁ Plasticity preserved: FST checkpoints respond better to additional RL on new tasks than RL-only ones
⦁ Continual learning across changing tasks (HoVer → CodeIO → Physics) where RL stalls the moment the task switches
FST is a direction towards:
⦁ Addressing RL's pain points: entropy collapse, sparse rewards, long-horizon exploration
⦁ Providing a clean channel for rich feedback into weight updates
⦁ Demonstrating model-harness co-evolution
⦁ Discovery: Using fast context updates for broad exploration, while leveraging a continually improving model.
Check out the full thread below:
Quoting @KushaSareen
Can LLMs adapt continually without losing base skills?
Fast-Slow Training (FST) pairs "slow" weights with "fast" context.
FST vs. RL:
• 3x more sample-efficient
• Higher performance ceiling
• Less KL drift (better plasticity)
• Continual learning: succeeds where RL stalls
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2054579357247537152/img/_0KT50Kp8DmblnqR.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2054579357247537152/vid/avc1/480x270/qQMlUjXJu8tDTbi4.mp4?tag=27
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HINVH9nXsAAAgXJ.jpg
clean_summary:
Learning from rich textual feedback, such as errors, traces, and partial reasoning, outperforms scalar reward alone for large language model optimization. GEPA demonstrated this for context-space optimization, achieving frontier results at a fraction of the cost of reinforcement learning. However, context-only optimization is limited by the base model's capability ceiling, so weight updates can push further.

Fast-Slow Training (FST) is a new approach that interleaves two optimization loops: a fast loop updating the context layer with rich rollout feedback, creating a dynamic scratchpad of task-relevant information; and a slow loop performing RL updates on the model parameters conditioned on this evolving context. This division allows the model to be more sample-efficient, with about three times the efficiency of RL on math, code, and physics reasoning, and reduces KL divergence from the base model by around 70% at similar accuracy. FST also preserves plasticity, enabling better adaptation to new tasks and continual learning where RL often stalls.

FST addresses common RL challenges like entropy collapse and sparse rewards, providing a clear channel for rich feedback and encouraging model-harness co-evolution. It leverages fast context updates for exploration while the model parameters improve continually, pushing the frontier of scalable, adaptable LLM training.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: RLM iteratively builds an interface to play Pokemon Red in under 5 hours
summary:
A fun 48-hour run of letting an RLM iteratively building the interface for an RLM to play Pokemon Red (sneak peak of some fun things cooking at @PrimeIntellect😄). The interface generating RLM was just tasked with getting the RLM (same scaffold) to beat the game in under 5 hours wall-clock time.
I originally expected the RLM to design some components used in Gemini Plays Pokemon like an extra map, an interface to parse the screen, etc., design low-level policies that would run fast on the emulator, and also design a good prompt and strategy around the RLM to use sub-agents to explore game state with checkpointing, use RNG manipulation in its favor, etc.
Instead the RLM eventually just decided to give the RLM a `write_memory` tool, which the RLM player decided to use to 1) warp the player immediately to the Elite 4; 2) give itself a level 100 Mewtwo (which it mistakes to be a Ponyta due to weird Pokedex ID vs. internal ID); 3) give itself $999999; 4) give itself all 8 badges by setting the right flag. It then went ahead and destroyed the Elite 4 and Blue and beat the game in record time :p
You'll also notice in the video there's weird backtracking and frame-skipping, this happens because it also did incorporate the strategy of launching sub-agents to explore action trajectories, but had a strange way of saving the frames and recording them (so you see the result of several sub-agent explorations).
We'll have some more funny and cool RLM demos soon, but it's cool to see RLMs work as general-purpose agents (both the coding agent that designs the interface and the game-playing agent itself)!
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2055115708036530176/img/929hUdCYMHnvACMa.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2055115708036530176/vid/avc1/320x456/89y5r7EluQQ0Y2i2.mp4?tag=27
clean_summary: Omar Khattab describes a 48-hour experiment where a reinforcement learning model (RLM) was tasked with creating an interface for an RLM to play Pokemon Red. Instead of designing components like maps or parsing interfaces, the RLM eventually used a `write_memory` tool to warp directly to the Elite 4, give itself a level 100 Mewtwo, max out money, and obtain all badges. It then defeated the Elite 4 and finished the game in record time. The process involved backtracking and frame-skipping due to exploring action trajectories with sub-agents. This demo shows how RLMs can function as general-purpose agents, both for designing interfaces and for playing games.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: MIT introduces Pedagogical RL to improve training with reasoning traces
summary:
MIT just released a new RL method called Pedagogical RL.
The main lesson -> correct reasoning traces can still be bad training data.
It is a similar concept to teaching someone backprop.
Say you have a tiny computation graph:
z = wx + b
a = ReLU(z)
L = (a - y)²
If you already understand backprop, you can jump straight to the gradient:
dL/dw = 2(a - y) · 1[z > 0] · x
The answer is correct but it skips the reasoning process.
To get there, you need to break the computation into local pieces:
dL/da = 2(a - y)
da/dz = 1[z > 0]
dz/dw = x
Then backprop is just composing those local derivatives backward through the graph:
dL/dw = dL/da · da/dz · dz/dw = 2(a - y) · 1[z > 0] · x
Showing a student the final gradient does not teach them how to find gradients on new graphs.
Even telling them “just use the chain rule” may be too large of a jump if they do not understand how to decompose the computation into intermediate nodes and local derivatives.
Reasoning RL has the same failure mode.
A rollout can pass the verifier while containing one step the student model basically never would have taken.
The trajectory gets the answer right, but the learning signal is brittle because the path is too far from the student’s current policy.
Pedagogical RL trains a privileged teacher that knows the answer, then rewards it for producing trajectories that stay learnable for the student.
The trick is to use a spike-aware reward. It penalizes single huge surprise gaps in the trajectory, even when the average likelihood of the trajectory looks fine.
Then the student learns with surprisal-gated imitation, where teacher tokens that are still too surprising get downweighted.
The teacher is learning how to teach at the student’s current level.
Pedagogical RL makes RL more efficient by efficiently selecting trajectories the student is most ready to learn from.
Less waiting for the model to get lucky rollouts. More training signal from examples that meet the student where it is.
Full blog in comments
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HInW1eUbUAASMxA.jpg
clean_summary:
MIT has released a new reinforcement learning method called Pedagogical RL, which addresses the problem that correct reasoning traces can still be poor training data if they are too brittle or far from the current policy.

This method involves training a teacher model that knows the correct answer and rewards trajectories that are learnable for the student, using a spike-aware reward to penalize large surprises. The student then learns through surprisal-gated imitation, downweighting overly surprising tokens, enabling more efficient learning from examples that match its current level. Pedagogical RL aims to make RL training more effective by selecting trajectories that the student is most ready to learn from, reducing wasted rollouts and increasing useful training signals.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Pedagogical reinforcement learning with spike-aware learnability rewards
summary:
Omar Khattab’s lab at MIT strikes again!
Pedagogical RL -
Today, RL relies on pure entropy to sample new trajectories. This is pretty inefficient, and also caps performance at what is already within stumbling range of the current model.
In almost every RL setup, we’re leaving valuable information from the judge or reward signal on the table, that could drastically improve sampling.
The solution, naturally, is to roll out a teacher model with privileged information. The problem is, this will be so off-policy from the model and could be cheating, that training will collapse.
Thus, to fully achieve this objective, the team defines a new spike-aware learnability reward - disproportionately penalizing high-surprise tokens from the students perspective, to RL train a teacher. AND they also surprisal-gate in the eventual loss function when reaching the student on these generated trajectories.
Altogether, this leads to significantly faster convergence than any other method compared (GRPO, OPSD) which is quite impressive.
Authors: @SOURADIPCHAKR18 @NoahZiems @furongh @Meng_CS @amritsinghbedi3 @lateinteraction
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIsNfQDb0AAGrcn.jpg
clean_summary: Omar Khattab’s lab at MIT introduces a new approach to reinforcement learning that improves sampling efficiency by using a teacher model with privileged information. Instead of relying solely on entropy to generate trajectories, they penalize high-surprise tokens from the student's perspective, encouraging the teacher to guide the student more effectively. This method leads to significantly faster convergence compared to previous techniques like GRPO and OPSD, demonstrating a promising direction for more efficient RL training.

summary:
this is why i love DSPy and RLM they are ideas that democratize AI
they let smaller models go further, they help us be efficient and extract more value from what we have, from what cannot be taken away
Quoting @natolambert
For a long time, academic researchers being at the cutting edge of new technologies has been a great social equilibrium. Neutral, unbiased technologists have been the people to spread new ideas to the world.
As AI research takes off in velocity, it is also going behind closed doors. The tech industry has sewed distrust, and now they are the ones trying to tell the world about incredible changes coming. It's a big loss to a form of social contract in America.
There's been a history of scientists helping society understand new technologies. There is a public service in the culture of science that I want to see continue.
It's being exacerbated by feelings of FOMO, especially finically driven, where I'm seeing many people who previously wanted to be professors -- and likely still do deep down -- feel a need to conform and chase money, in a pocket of industry. I get it, I grapple with this.
For those with a safety net, there will be great returns to some who choose to zag, and try to build something good, for people who need something different. For me, this is building interesting, fully-open models, to show what you can do with a variety of open weight sizes.
Yes, AI's immediate future is dictated by the frontier, but it's long-term trajectory still deeply includes academic institutions and open science. Knowledge will always diffuse, but to whom?
As of today, I think China is positioned to be the global home of AI research in a few years. The home of research is where ideas are accessible, spread rapdily, and are nurtured. The U.S. seems to be unwinding many institutions and relationships.
The largest returns go to people who build something differentiated, at least in reputation, and a lot of people are not being shown that this path exists.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Great work on Vector Policy Optimization (VPO)
summary:
Great work on Vector Policy Optimization (VPO).
The standard scalar-reward view of post-training is inherently lossy: compressing a trajectory into one number discards a lot of useful structure, such as which sub-goals were met, where the reasoning failed, and what tradeoffs were made.
VPO makes this point concretely by using vector-valued rewards to train models that cover different regions of the reward space. This is especially relevant as inference-time search becomes more important where diversity is not just beneficial but directly useful.
This also connects to the success of methods like GEPA: richer feedback representations, whether vector-valued or semantic/natural-language, can carry much more optimization signal than sparse scalar rewards. More broadly, we may need to rethink “reward” as a structured feedback object rather than a single compressed scalar.
Quoting @RyanBoldi

clean_summary:
Great work on Vector Policy Optimization (VPO). The standard scalar-reward view of post-training is inherently lossy, as compressing a trajectory into one number discards useful information like sub-goals, reasoning failures, and tradeoffs.

VPO addresses this by using vector-valued rewards to train models that explore different regions of the reward space. This approach is especially relevant as inference-time search becomes more important, where diversity is directly useful. It also relates to methods like GEPA, which leverage richer feedback representations—whether vector-valued or semantic—to provide more optimization signal than sparse scalar rewards. Overall, this suggests we may need to rethink reward as a structured feedback object rather than a single scalar.

Compared with strong baselines, including RAG, Compaction Agents, and SOTA prompt-learning frameworks, PEEK dominates the cost–quality Pareto frontier: achieving +6.3–34.0% in quality, with fewer iterations and lower cost.
Paper:
GitHub:
More in the thread below! (1/N)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIyjPBHW0AAHdmu.jpg
clean_summary:
Recent agentic systems like Claude Code, Codex, and RLM move context out of the prompt into external environments, such as files, to maintain long-term knowledge about their goals and functions. Surprisingly, systems that use external environments perform much better when given a small, fixed-size, in-context, agent-managed cache that 'peeks into' these environments.

The paper introduces PEEK, a system for building and maintaining an orientation cache for LLM agents, which outperforms strong baselines including RAG, Compaction Agents, and state-of-the-art prompt-learning frameworks by achieving 6.3 to 34.0% higher quality at lower costs and fewer iterations. This approach demonstrates a cost-effective way to enhance long-context LLM agent performance.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Critique of on-policy distillation as an instructional method
summary:
extremely informal rant: on-policy distillation is so awkward and frankly just super overrated.
why so? well, you'd absolutely hate to be the teacher in an OPD or OPSD setting.
imagine trying to teach an aspiring undergrad how to do research by... just asking them to do it, and then passively watching them wander for countless hours doing something bogus.
after they're completely done, your only tool is to replay their bogus trajectory as-is and offer them 1 token of correction starting from every (rather unhelpful) state they arrive at.
or imagine trying to teach someone how to drive to the nearest Target. so you throw them into a car and ask them to do that, and you just... let them mess around in random directions. after they're done, you can't actually help them drive anywhere, you're just offering 1-step of 10-millisecond steering guidance for them to distill, from every (bad) state they arrived at!
in OPD, the teacher is forced to stare at absolute nonsense attempts and can't course-correct at all. i can believe this to work in cases where the problems with trajectories are rather sparse and repetitive, and it *is* better than on-policy RL in many such cases.
but i think Pedagogical RL, which is a form of "controllably off-policy" self-distillation is conceptually a much more powerful direction.
the teacher's job is to actually instruct and to diverge from student's likely actions to the (smallest) necessary extent for success.
clean_summary:
This tweet criticizes on-policy distillation (OPD) and on-policy supervised distillation (OPSD) as overly awkward and overrated. It compares OPD to a teacher passively watching a student wander aimlessly or trying to teach driving by letting someone mess around in a car with minimal guidance, which makes it hard to effectively correct or guide the learner.

The tweet suggests that in OPD, the teacher cannot course-correct during the process and is limited to small corrections after the fact, which is inefficient. While it may work in cases with sparse and repetitive trajectory errors, the author advocates for Pedagogical Reinforcement Learning, a form of 'controllably off-policy' self-distillation, where the teacher actively instructs and diverges from the student's actions only as much as necessary for success, making it a more powerful approach.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
Thanks for sharing our work @lateinteraction @sum!
The idea is extremely simple:
- multi-vector retrieval is so costly that it often needs k-means to categorize tokens first;
- k-means is essentially a top-1 sparse coding method (n-dim dense->1-dim cluster id), which means it loses a lot of information in the middle stage;
- if we need sparsity anyway, why dont we just do a 1-stage, e2e sparse coding (n-dim dense in, k-dim sparse out)? then it becomes single-stage sparse retrieval (SSR );
- thus, SSR with topk (k=32 by default) is strictly better than multi-stage ones from an information-theoretic perspective, since it avoids this top-1 lossy k-means bottleneck.
In fact, SSR is essentially a "CSR-v3", part of the "learned sparse retrieval" thread of work we explored in the last 2 years:
- CSR (ICML'25 oral): unsupervised SAE + contrastive learning is superior for efficient retrieval;
- CSR-v2 (ICLR'26): ultra-sparse CSR with k as small as 2/4, 4x more efficient than CSRv1;
- SSR (v3, ICML'26): introduces CSR to token-level, showing sparse embedding can outperform dense ones at multi-vector regimes as well.
We actually submitted a "v4" recently that further cultivates the nice properties of sparse embeddings. Stay tuned!

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
clean_title: Stanford's free web-based research assistant STORM predates OpenAI and Perplexity tools
summary:
Well, maybe the real point is that interesting new research and product directions get explored by us and other university research labs first!
🤔
Quoting @heynavtoor
Stanford built a free version of Deep Research a year before OpenAI and Perplexity launched theirs.
Six researchers at Stanford published it: Yijia Shao, Yucheng Jiang, Theodore Kanell, Peter Xu, Omar Khattab, and Professor Monica Lam.
The paper went up in February 2024. OpenAI launched their $200 a month Deep Research in February 2025. Perplexity launched theirs at $20 a month two weeks later.
The Stanford version was free the whole time.
It's called STORM. You type a topic. It searches the web, reads sources, and writes you a full report with citations.
Most AI tools answer your question by guessing what you want. STORM does something different. It looks at existing articles on similar topics, figures out what questions are missing, and asks itself follow-ups like a journalist interviewing an expert. The answers become the report.
What you get:
- A topic-to-report engine that cites every source
- A live web demo, no install needed
- A second version called Co-STORM that lets you join in and steer the research
- A mind map that grows as the AI learns
- Plug in any AI model you want, including local ones
Try it at No login. No subscription. Over 70,000 people already have.
28,292 stars on GitHub. 2,578 forks. MIT license, free for any use.
OpenAI charges $200 a month. Perplexity charges $20 a month. Stanford charges nothing, ships the source code, and has the peer-reviewed paper to back the work.
The paper is older than the paywall.
(Link in the comments)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJz-fF0aMAAJrVS.jpg
clean_summary: Interesting new research and product directions often emerge first from university labs. Stanford built a free version of Deep Research called STORM a year before OpenAI and Perplexity launched their paid versions. STORM searches the web, reads sources, and writes full reports with citations by analyzing existing articles, identifying missing questions, and asking follow-ups like a journalist. It offers a topic-to-report engine, a live web demo, a collaborative version called Co-STORM, and a growing mind map, all without login or subscription. Stanford's open-source tool is backed by a peer-reviewed paper and is freely available, while competitors charge monthly fees.
